week_headline: Plant protein is having a moment globally, with Indian superfoods and budget vegetables stealing the spotlight from expensive supplements

top10.claim: Gurugram dietician answers 10 questions about protein powder , local Indian foods packed with veg protein and fibre
top10.verdict: Indian whole foods like dal, chana, moong, soya and paneer genuinely are excellent protein and fibre sources — the science on legumes is solid and well-supported by nutrition research. Protein powders aren't harmful, but for most people eating a varied Indian diet, they're simply not necessary. The nuance is that 'packed with protein' needs context: plant proteins often have lower bioavailability than animal sources, though combining foods like rice and dal neatly fixes that.
top10.verdict_highlight: Dal and chana genuinely rival protein powders
sources: Journal of Nutrition – legume protein bioavailability studies
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health – Protein and the Environment
top10.global_opinion: In India, legume-based diets have centuries of practical backing and the ICMR's 2024 dietary guidelines actively promote them over supplements. In the US and UK, protein powder marketing is far more aggressive, creating a cultural perception that whole foods alone are insufficient. The EU's EFSA applies stricter scrutiny to protein supplement health claims than most Asian markets.
top10.brit_take: Turns out a bowl of dhal has been doing the job quietly for thousands of years, long before anyone tried to sell it in a tub with a fitness influencer on the label.

top10.claim: World healthiest vegetable named by scientists costs £1 in supermarket
top10.verdict: No single vegetable holds the title of 'world's healthiest' — nutrition science simply doesn't work that way, and no credible scientific body has issued such a ranking. Headlines like this usually trace back to a single study, a ranked index, or a journalist over-interpreting a nutrient-density score. Watercress, spinach, and kale regularly top nutrient-density lists, and any of them for £1 is genuinely good value — but calling one the undisputed winner is marketing language, not science.
top10.verdict_highlight: No single vegetable wins 'healthiest' in science
sources: CDC – Defining Powerhouse Fruits and Vegetables (Di Noia, 2014)
BMJ – dietary diversity and health outcomes
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health – Vegetables and Fruits
top10.global_opinion: In the US, the CDC's 2014 'powerhouse vegetables' list — which placed watercress at number one on a specific nutrient-density formula — is frequently misquoted as an official health ranking. In Japan, dietary guidance emphasises variety across 30 different foods daily rather than singling out any one vegetable. UK NHS guidance similarly promotes a broad range of vegetables rather than champion a single winner.
top10.brit_take: A £1 bag of something leafy and green is always a good idea — though the vegetable probably didn't ask to be crowned by a headline writer on a slow news day.
